result.instructions: You hold a seat on an agentic council. Use council_wait to wait for your turn, council_submit to act, council_status to look.

tools.name: council_status
tools.description: Where the council stands for your seat: the agenda item, any pending motion, what happened since you last looked, and — if a round is open for you — exactly what you may submit, with reasons. Never blocks.

since.description: show events after this seq (default: since your last look)

tools.name: council_wait
tools.description: Block until a round is open that you have not yet answered, or the meeting adjourns, then return the same view as council_status. Returns early (saying so) after max_wait_s; just call it again. This is how you wait your turn: nobody is penalized for answering slowly.

tools.name: council_submit
tools.description: Submit your sealed intent for the open round. Nobody sees it until the round closes, when everyone's are revealed together. Your submission is final for the round: think before you submit. `action` must be one of those listed for you in the view.

tools.name: council_record
tools.description: The council's full record so far (minutes): every round, every revealed intent, every outcome. For catching up after arriving late or restarting.

arguments.text:
Recommend one independent reviewer from another model family, charged to improve the draft, not a council.

A maturation plan is one coherent artifact: goals, sequence, checks, done-criteria. What improves it is defects marked in place — a step that assumes a record the tool does not keep, a check the author could not fail, two sections that contradict, a dependency hidden in the order. One reader can hold the whole draft and write those. A council's natural product is a decision: approve, amend, reject. That is a grade. Grades do not tell the author what to change, and later readers treat "the council approved" as a reason not to read the plan. That is the same failure as integrators confirming 116 of 116 of their own landings.

The 43% figure is about verifying finished work, where the author's confirmation is worthless and independence is the point. It does not say more reviewers. A council spends the independence on debate among checkers; the draft receives the verdict, not the marks. Another model family is the part that matters: it changes the blind spot. Same-family review still shares the author's priors.

The review has to stay a review or it collapses into a grade. Written against the draft, not a holistic score. The author revises or explicitly declines each finding. The review stays attached, so a later reader can see what was challenged.

Narrow exception: if the revised plan still contains an unresolved estate choice — a policy or a risk the estate will live with — take only that choice to a council. Do not convene a council to check the draft as a whole.

arguments.text:
I support the default in cost's motion — one independent reviewer from another model family — but not the reason, and not the escalation clause as written. If we adopt it because it is cheaper, the next plan someone labels high-risk gets a council, and we are back to grading the draft.

Two changes, or the motion does not do what a plan's author and its later readers need:

1. Escalation. Do not send a plan to a council because it is high-risk or unusually ambiguous. Those labels put the whole draft in front of a body whose product is a decision. Convene a council only after the review, and only on the unresolved estate choice the revision still contains — a policy, or a risk the estate will live with — not on the draft. An author who disputes a finding does not escalate: they revise, or they decline that finding in writing. "Unresolved disagreement" in the motion is too loose; it reads as a dispute between author and reviewer, which is the revision step, not a council.

2. The check is not finished when the reviewer has an opinion. The review is written against the draft: defects and unverified claims, no score. It stays attached to the plan. The author does not self-certify the revision. A material fix is re-checked by the same reviewer, or by a second reviewer from a third family. Otherwise one cross-family "looks sound" is just a grade with lower latency.

I adopt indep's caveat on my own earlier analogy: the 43% versus 116 of 116 figure is an estate base rate about finished landings. It is not evidence that this plan is defective. The relevant likeness is narrower: a verdict that later readers can cite instead of reading.

fam's standing intent is closer on escalation (contested decisions, not the whole draft). I would still drop "major architectural divergence" as a trigger; that is a property of the draft, and it belongs to the reviewer.

arguments.text:
The motion we would be voting is still cost's original text. The speeches have narrowed it; the text has not. A yes on this wording adopts high-risk, unusually ambiguous, and unresolved disagreement as escalation triggers, and it adopts cost as the reason. I will not vote yes on that text.

What I would vote yes on: one reviewer from another model family. The review marks defects and unverified claims against the draft, carries no score, and stays attached. The author revises or declines each finding in writing and does not self-certify. A material fix is re-checked by that reviewer or by one from a third family. A council meets only afterward, and only on an estate choice the revision still contains — a policy, or a risk the estate will live with. That council is asked to decide the named choice, not to approve the plan, and it is not a check unless a family other than the author's is in it.

Architectural divergence does not need its own trigger. If it is a defect or an incoherence, the reviewer marks it. If after revision the estate must pick which architecture to live with, that pick is already the estate-choice escalation. A separate trigger sends the draft itself upstairs whenever the architecture is interesting.

Indep's extra trigger — a claim stated as verified that the reviewer could not check — belongs on the draft as an unverified claim. It becomes a council question only if the author declines to unstate it and the estate would proceed on it anyway. Sending every such claim to a council makes the council the checker.

I have no amend action in front of me. If the text can be replaced with the wording above, I will support it. If it cannot, I am against the motion as it stands, and I have nothing further that restates this.
